newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Air Ukraine to choose Western plane partner in Jan.
newsitem.headline: Air Ukraine to choose Western plane partner in Jan.

text.p: Ukrainian airline Air Ukraine will decide next month whether to opt for Europe or America to replace its ageing Soviet-era fleet, a senior company official said on Friday.
But plans to choose this month between U.S. Boeing Corp and Airbus Industrie have come to nothing.
"The situation is not clear at all. There is complete silence on the issue," the official told Reuters.

The plans to lease or buy Western-made planes is part of a bold project by the state-owned airline to cope with strong potential in the former Soviet republic, which has lifted Soviet-era travel restrictions and allowed people to go abroad.
"The Ukrainian aviation market is growing and has amazing prospects," a transport ministry official said, noting that business travel and tourism were both on the upswing.
"In the coming decade Ukraine's needs will stand at several dozen Western-made planes."

Air Ukraine, which in 1991 inherited planes left on its territory by Soviet flag-carrier Aeroflot after the collapse of Soviet Union, has a fleet of 240 planes, mostly Soviet-made Tupolev 154 and 134s, Antonov 24s and Yakovlev 40 and 42s.
It also flies one Boeing 737s.
But more than half the Soviet-made planes are grounded and Air Ukraine started its search for a Western partner this year.
Since then Ukraine has paid witness to an elaborate courtship dance from the two big plane makers as well as indecision and secrecy from the Ukrainian authorities.

The airline said in July it would choose Boeing for Transatlantic routes from 1997. Two months later it said it would lease Airbus planes, and Airbus Industrie began conducting demonstration flights over Kiev.
The airline now flies to New York and Toronto with Soviet-made Il-62 jets, and it plans non-stop flights to Chicago and Washington soon, adding Los Angeles and Miami by 1999.
It also serves Ukraine, the former Soviet Union, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, India and China.

Interfax-Ukraine news agency said this week that Boeing was ready to sell Air Ukraine one 767-200ER long-range jet with a 216-passenger capacity for $60-65 million, and one mid-range Boeing-737-300 for 135 passengers for $30.2 million.
Airbus Industrie proposed leasing two long-range A310-300 with a 183-passenger-capacity for $370,000-$400,000 monthly, and one mid-range A32O-200 at 164 people for $270,000 per month.
The European aircraft-builder's scheme also foresees selling its newly-designed Airbus 330-200 with a 293-passenger capacity for $75-79 million each in 1999.
The company is also ready to give a $15.5 million, two-year credit over 12 years, $700,000 to retrain Air Ukraine personnel, and to spend $1 million to modernise the carrier's fleet.

"The struggle for Ukrainian skies continues and, sadly, it's mostly under the carpet," the mass-circulation daily Kievskiye Vedomosti wrote recently. "It is no secret the two companies have very powerful lobbies in Kiev."

Observers say a U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) decision to prohibit Il-62 planes from landing in the United States by April 1 because they were "technologically and ecologically unsound" could speed up the decision.

"We were supposed to send pilots for an Airbus training course. They haven't gone because there was no final decision," the Air Ukraine official said. "But if we start in January we still could still...begin flying by April."
